The Bad Lands Cow Boy. Volume 1, Number 34. LITTLE MISSOURI, MEDORA P. O., DAK., SEPTEMBER 25, 1884. Price $2.00 per Year.

BAD LANDS COW BOY, BY A. T. PACKARD. The Cow Boy is not published for fun, but for $2 per year. Advertising Rates made known on application. Standing Advertisements payable quarterly. Transient Advertisements and all Job work, money in sight. Address all communications to THE BAD LANDS COW BOY, MEDORA, DAKOTA. articles.headline: The Convention.
articles.text:
Pursuant to a call issued by the chairman of the county central committee a republican convention was held in Robert's hall at Medora on last Monday evening, September 22, 1884, for the purpose of electing two delegates to represent Billings county at the legislative convention to be held at Bismarck on October 15.

The convention was called to order by J. C. Fisher, chairman of the county central committee.

Moved that L. H. Palmer act as secretary.

Here a point of order was raised that the call should be first read and a permanent chairman elected. The chair overruled the point, maintaining that he held the office by virtue of former election. L. H. Palmer was then made secretary.

The secretary read the call as published.

A motion was then made and seconded that Robt. Roberts be elected by acclamation as one of the delegates.

F. H. Ertel offered as an amendment that they proceed to ballot for delegates and the two receiving the highest number of votes be declared elected, and urged it in the interest of fairness to all, but finally withdrew the amendment. The original motion prevailed and Mr. Roberts was duly elected without a dissenting vote.

J. C. Fisher and L. C. Hay were then put in nomination.

Mr. Hay declined the honor, and stated that he had not come to the convention to seek the delegateship, and explained his position in reference to the Belfield convention.

J. C. Fisher was then elected delegate without dissent.

F. H. Ertel offered the following resolution, which was unanimously adopted and the convention adjourned sine die:

Whereas, The Mandan Pioneer upon various occasions has presumed upon the good sense and competent judgement of the Republicans of Billings county, in trying to dictate to them through the columns of the paper, be it

Resolved, That grateful as the Republicans feel to the editors of said journal, for the deep interest taken in Billings county, the voters of Billings county feel sufficient confidence in themselves to manage their own affairs and assume all responsibility for their actions.

L. H. Palmer, Secretary.
articles.summary: Billings county Republicans met at Robert's hall, Medora, on Sept. 22 and chose Robt. Roberts and J. C. Fisher as delegates to the Bismarck legislative convention, and resolved against the Mandan Pioneer's dictation.

articles.text: The supreme court of Dakota has rendered a decision in the case of the territory against the capital commission, declaring that body a legal one and capable of exercising the powers given it by the legislature creating it. This finally settles the capital question and makes Bismarck legally what in fact it has been for some time, the seat of goverment for the territorry of Dakota.
articles.summary: The Dakota supreme court upheld the capital commission, confirming Bismarck as the territorial capital.

articles.headline: Certificate.
articles.text:
This certificate is drawn, signed and acknowledged by the parties hereto in order to conform to the requirements of the civil code of the territory of Dakota demanded of parties transacting business in said territory under a ficticious name or under a designation not showing the names of the persons interested as partners in said business.

We the undersigned hereby certify that we have this day entered into copartnership under the name of the "Medora Stage and Forwarding Company," and that:

1. Our full and true names are Arthur T. Packard and Erasmus Deffebach.

2. That our residence is at the town of Medora in the county of Billings, in the territory of Dakota.

3. That the principal place of business of said partnership is at the town of Medora aforesaid.

Dated, Medora, D. T., Sept. 8, 1884.

Arthur T. Packard.
Erasmus Deffebach.

Witness: Frank B. Allen.

Territory of Dakota, County of Billings, } ss.

On this eighth day of September, 1884, before me, Frank B. Allen, a notary public, personally appeared Arthur T. Packard and Erasmus Deffebach, to me well known as the same persons described in and who executed the foregoing instrument, and acknowledged that they executed the same freely and voluntarily for the uses and purposes therein expressed and specified.

In witness whereof I have hereunto set my hand and official seal at said county the day and year above written.

[Seal] Frank B. Allen, Notary Public.
articles.summary: Certificate of copartnership, dated Sept. 8, 1884, forming the Medora Stage and Forwarding Company by Arthur T. Packard and Erasmus Deffebach, acknowledged before notary Frank B. Allen.

The above reward will be paid for information leading to the arrest of any person or persons setting fire to the grass in the cattle sections of Western Dakota.

N. P. Ref. Car Co.

articles.text:
The above reward will be paid for the return of the following stock or a proportionate reward will be paid for the return of any of them. The stock consists of the following horses:

One bay mare, one brown mare and one roan mare, all young and branded double or reverse P on left shoulder as advertised in our brand columns. Also one light sorrel pony, white legs and face and branded NC on left shoulder and triangle JP on right shoulder also as advertised in our brand columns.

Gregor Lang,

articles.text: It is claimed that there are $10,000,000 worth of Jersey cattle in this country.
articles.summary: Short item on the value of Jersey cattle in the country.

articles.text: Hog cholera continues emptying the pens in the western part of Sarpy county, Nebraska.
articles.summary: Hog cholera in Sarpy county, Nebraska.

articles.text: A mare mule recently gave birth to a colt in the State of Oaxaca. The colt died shortly after birth.
articles.summary: A mare mule foaled in Oaxaca; the colt died.

articles.text: The highest valuation of cattle in Colorado per head for taxation is $19.77; the average for the state is less than $15.00.
articles.summary: Colorado cattle tax valuations.

articles.text: It is estimated that there is one sheep in the United States to every thirty-four acres of territory. In England the rate is one to one and a half acres.
articles.summary: Sheep per acre in the U.S. and England.

articles.text: The shipment of cattle from here to Chicago has commenced again in good earnest, and between now and the 5th of October no less than 500 carloads of prime beeves will be loaded at this point.—[Dickinson Press.
articles.summary: The Dickinson Press reported heavy cattle shipments from Dickinson to Chicago, with 500 carloads expected before Oct. 5.

articles.text: Twelve hundred head of cattle bearing the S D brand of S. Doyle arrived here yesterday in charge of about a dozen cow boys, who have brought the herd from the west and are taking the stock to a range fifty miles east of Glendive.—[Yellowstone Journal.
articles.summary: Yellowstone Journal: S. Doyle's 1,200 SD-branded cattle arrived from the west in charge of a dozen cowboys, bound for a range east of Glendive.

articles.text: A Northern Pacific official denies that stockmen seek the rival roads for their shipments. He claims that the Northern Pacific is ahead of the others in offering inducements to shippers, and that this will be abundantly shown when at the end of the season the figures are published—[Mandan Pioneer.
articles.summary: A Northern Pacific official denied stockmen favored rival roads for shipments.

articles.text: It is often claimed and supposed by many that stockmen frame and influence legislation to suit them. The fact is, stockmen prosper in spite of adverse legislation. The stockman did best when lands were governed by no laws. They would as soon influence Indians as legislators.—[Tex. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Clipping arguing stockmen do not shape legislation.

articles.text: Cocoanut oil cake is used in Java quite largely for live-stock food. It is made by crushing the kernel and extracting from it the oil by means of hydraulic pressure. The refuse left after the extraction of the oil is then pressed into cakes, and is eagerly devoured by cattle, who are said to fatten very rapidly on it.
articles.summary: Coconut oil cake as cattle feed in Java.

articles.text: Denver, Colorado, is fixing for a refrigerator establishment on a grand scale. The preliminary steps include securing a large pasture for grazing and feeding beeves purchased, so as not to be purchasing from hand to mouth, so to speak. They seem to recognize that capital is required. It should be a success.—[Tex. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Planned refrigerator beef establishment at Denver.

articles.text: A manager of a New Mexico cattle company who uses the Shorthorn as a cross, on account of their hardihood, is about to use the Spanish as another cross, on account of their gentleness. There is reason in all things and the hardy Shorthorn and gentle Texan are entitled to their honors—even if not exactly fitting them.—[Tex. L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Crossbreeding plans of a New Mexico cattle company.

articles.text: For mutton, Professor Brown, of the Guelph Agricultural College, Canada, says in his experience Leicester sheep are ahead of all others in putting on flesh in the shortest time. In early maturing he gives the following as the result of personal observations: Leicesters, Southdown cross, Leicester cross, Oxford Down cross, Cotswold being the slowest.—[Kan. City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Professor Brown of Guelph on fast-maturing mutton sheep.

articles.text: A disease has appeared among the cattle in the northwestern part of Osage county, Kan., and several fatal cases are reported. The owners of the cattle do not know what the disease is, but a quarantine has been established to prevent its spread. After being affected, the cattle only live a day or two. Drowsiness, costiveness and bloody discharges are its main symptoms.—[Kan. City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Fatal cattle disease and quarantine in Osage county, Kansas.

articles.text: The amount of wool shipped from Fort Benton and vicinity during the past season aggregates 795,722 pounds. Of this amount 689,558 pounds were shipped from Fort Benton; 4,681 pounds from the coal banks; 86,136 pounds from Judith; 15,346 pounds from Rocky Point. These shipments were all made by the Power line of steamers, the Benton on two trips carrying 997 bales, the Batchelor on three trips 1,427 and the Helena on one trip, 428.—[Exchange.
articles.summary: Fort Benton area wool shipments for the season.

articles.text: The Continental Land and Cattle Company, one of the wealthiest concerns of the kind in the country, shipped a train load of cattle from this place yesterday that were all black and averaged in weight about eleven hundred pounds each. It was a novelty, being the first train of black cattle ever shipped from Montana or Dakota territories. They were the selection of John N. Simpson and A. B. Combes. The company shipped from here this week over sixty carloads of fine fat cattle.—[Dickinson Press.
articles.summary: Dickinson Press: the Continental Land and Cattle Company shipped the first trainload of black cattle from Montana or Dakota, and over sixty carloads that week.

articles.text: The day has gone by when size is considered before quality in cattle. The big, rough hulks of enormous weights are passed by in the sale pens for smaller, but smoother and neater cattle. These compactly built, smooth-bodied beeves are subject to less shrinkage both in shipping and turning into beef, require less feed, and give evidence of possessing a greater hardiness of constitution, and are by all means the most profitable for the farmer to handle. If farmers, in selecting cattle either for breeding or feeding purposes, would be assured that they are obtaining stock that will be profitable, they must bear these points in mind, and select more for quality than for size.—[Exchange.
articles.summary: Exchange item urging quality over size in cattle.

articles.text: A telegram from Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory, under date of Sept. 16, says: In accordance with the governor's proclamation and the law of Wyoming, the territorial veterinarian and the executive committee of the stock association to-day issued a circular to railroads and the public generally, stating that no cattle brought from the States here will be admitted without passing a quarantine of ninety days or longer, as may be judged necessary. This action is taken in view of the recognized fact that a contagious disease of a dangerous character exists in eastern localities, and is made thus public to save loss and detention to shippers and the possibility of unintentional violation by railroads or individuals.—[Kansas City L. S. Indicator.
articles.summary: Wyoming imposed a 90-day quarantine on cattle from the States (Cheyenne, Sept. 16).

articles.text: The Union Mutual Live Stock association have filed articles of incorporation with the register of deeds. The object of the association is stated to be "one of charity, benevolence and mutual assistance among its members, and to indemnify each other by mutual assessments for the loss by death or disablement of horses, mules and cattle." The corporation is to commence Sept. 24, and continue fifty years. The requirements of membership are: First, the payment of one dollar annual dues on each animal; second, an admission fee of 1 per cent. of the affixed value of each animal; third, the payment of one-half per cent. of the value of the animal on joining the association; fourth, one-half the value of each animal insured upon the death of any animal belonging to a member. The articles are signed by William Uril, J. H. Hasty, Charles H. Penrith and J. W. Molyneaux.—[Pioneer Press.
articles.summary: Incorporation of the Union Mutual Live Stock association.

articles.text: The following is a distressing picture drawn in a dispatch with reference to the suffering of cattle that were shipped to New York city recently, during the hot spell, and clearly demonstrates the advantage of western slaughtered beef against these fever-heated animals: "Since Tuesday of last week 20 per cent. of the western cattle have died on the cars or immediately after being transferred to the stock yards. The soap factories are over-stocked with carcasses of steers, hogs and sheep bought at prices ranging from ten cents to fifty cents a head. Saturday night an Erie train load of cattle arrived at Hoboken too late for transfer by boat, and they remained in closely packed cars until Monday morning without food or drink, suffering terrible agony. When unloaded 20 per cent. were dead or dying while the living were in such a state of fever as to render them unfit for beef until cold weather. Two cars of the train were closely packed with calves, hogs and sheep. The sight was an atrocious one, while the cries of distress from the tortured creatures made spectators turn away. From the mouths of calves and sheep hung tongues swollen and blackened, while hogs were gnawing their own fat. All day long the sun beat down on the wretched animals, and the neighborhood heard little save the fearful wail. Only nineteen animals out of two car loads lived to be unloaded Monday morning."
articles.summary: Dispatch on cattle dying in transit to New York in the heat, cited as an argument for western-slaughtered beef.

articles.headline: The Horse Thief Fever.
articles.text: "Say Revenue, I tell you what it is; the Drag ain't no good after he's got a dose of horse thief fever. He don't represent worth a nickle. He'd better take a change of venue and make application for a sheep herder. He's coon-tailed and shows up nothing." Guess the Drag's about right and up near the line they give the rustlers, the fellows that get away with the horses, awful powerful medicine. Lariat rope and cottonwood tree, with tight cinch under the ear is a sure cure. An injection of cold lead from a Smith & Wesson syringe is a dandy where cottonwoods are scarce, and a lariat rope fast to a saddle horn with the loop around the patient's neck and the horse on a full gallop was frequently used by the Mexicans and Apaches. Yes, the remedy is severe, but recollect, you herders, the disease is powerful bad.—[Yellowetone Journal.
articles.summary: Yellowstone Journal piece on the summary 'cures' for horse thieves near the line.

articles.headline: Cattle Grazing on the Aleutians.
articles.text: Lieut. Fred Schwatka, of the United States army, who is for a few days stopping at the Leland Hotel, is enthusiastic over a scheme of his to form a company for growing cattle on the Aleutian Islands, in the North Pacific Ocean. Having had ample opportunity to study the advantages offered by these Islands he speaks in glowing terms of what might come of a large company properly managed. The islands contain about 3,000 square miles of excellent grazing lands, mostly low, but most of it 2,000 to 3,000 feet above the sea. The islands are small, and most of them are naturally divided in several places by bold mountain headlands that extend from the "backbone" range to the sea, forming natural fences. This would do away with the necessity of fencing bulls or branding cattle; two very important considerations. There is enough rich grass to form abundant feed all winter and hay can be cut anywhere on the low lands. The climate is mild on account of the warm Japan current. In more than 50 years the mercury has not gone lower than 1 degree above zero. The prevailing winter winds are southwesterly and summer winds are northwesterly, thus favoring boats that would transport beeves to the Pacific coast market. It is claimed that the cost of transportation to market would be within $5@10 per head; the latter price being ample to take beeves to San Francisco. The Lieutenant has no lack of faith in the scheme being a real bonanza, and the facts and figures he presents to back his faith are certainly very attractive.—[Drovers' Journal.
articles.summary: Drovers' Journal: Lieut. Fred Schwatka promoted a scheme for cattle ranching on the Aleutian Islands.

articles.text:
The political campaign is growing more brisk but will not get "red hot" until all the local candidates are in the field. These are relied upon to stir the pot and bring out a full vote.

It is said the "oldest inhabitant" does not recollect a more prolonged season of verdure in the northwest than the present. The season began somewhat later than usual, but has been uninterrupted by drouths or frost, and seems likely to last at least a month later.
articles.summary: Editorial notes on the warming local political campaign and an unusually long green season in the northwest.

Inside page set under the Cow Boy's editorial heading but carrying general and territorial matter: national editorial paragraphs (England's careless-gun cases, the French cholera scare, Senate seniority, Gen. Crook and the Apaches, Wolseley's Nile expedition); a long report with ballot tables of the Dakota Congressional Convention at Pierre that nominated Judge Oscar S. Gifford for Congress (the local column calls it 'a full report of the Pierre convention'); 'The Capital Question,' the territorial supreme court decision upholding the capital commission; a Yankton congregational college item; 'Got His Drink'; and 'Dakota News Notes.' Not transcribed.

Patent inside: Blaine and Logan Republican campaign matter, miscellany and humor ('Joking a Commander,' 'Secret of Gladstone's Vigor,' 'A Mother at Eleven Years of Age'), health hints, and patent-medicine and mail-order ads (Plymouth Clothing House, Parsons' Pills, Tutt's Pills, Cuticura, Perry Davis' Pain-Killer, Rockford Watches, Dr. Spinney, etc.).

articles.text: D. K. Wade came in from the ranch last Friday.
articles.summary: D. K. Wade came in from his ranch.

articles.text: The brick cottages are rapidly nearing completion.
articles.summary: The brick cottages in Medora were nearly finished.

articles.text: C. W. Sleeper returned from St. Paul last evening.
articles.summary: C. W. Sleeper returned from St. Paul.

articles.text: Alex. Metzger, of Bismarck, was in town Tuesday.
articles.summary: Alex. Metzger of Bismarck visited Medora.

articles.text: From thirty to thirty-five beeves a day are now being slaughtered at the abattoir.
articles.summary: The Medora abattoir was slaughtering 30 to 35 beeves a day.

articles.text: On the second page of this paper will be found a full report of the Pierre convention.
articles.summary: Note pointing readers to the page-2 report of the Pierre convention.

articles.text: T. J. Sharkey, traveling auditor of the Northern Pacific railroad, was in town yesterday.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific traveling auditor T. J. Sharkey visited Medora.

articles.text: The Baron and Baroness von Hoffmann returned from their western trip this morning in their special car.
articles.summary: The Baron and Baroness von Hoffmann returned from a western trip in their special car.

articles.text: F. H. Ertel, of the Bismarck Journal, and L. C. Hay, of Belfield, came up Monday evening to attend the convention.
articles.summary: F. H. Ertel and L. C. Hay came to Medora for the county convention.

articles.text: J. H. Kelly, of Duluth, now manipulates the electric-telegraph apparatus at the telegraph office, Mr. Smith having departed for Illinois.
articles.summary: J. H. Kelly of Duluth replaced Mr. Smith as Medora telegraph operator.

articles.text: Mr. A. E. Grymes, of New York, arrived in town Monday evening, and is visiting at the Marquis' residence. He is the father of J. F. Grimes, who is employed in the company's office.
articles.summary: A. E. Grymes of New York arrived to visit at the Marquis de Mores' residence.

articles.text: The Northern Pacific railroad surveyers, who have been in the vicinity some time for the purpose of locating the river, have completed their work and returned east last Sunday morning.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific surveyors finished work near Medora and went east.

articles.text: The dance at the Pyramid Park hotel last Friday evening proved to be one of the most enjoyable affairs of the season. The attendance was good and the music up to its usual standard of excellency.
articles.summary: A well-attended dance was held at the Pyramid Park hotel.

articles.text: D. O. Sweet and wife, of Forsythe, Mont., are among the new arrival in Medora. Mr. Sweet is looking for a location to engage in some business. He thinks the prospects are very bright, and it is safe to assert that he will remain with us.
articles.summary: D. O. Sweet and wife of Forsythe, Mont., arrived in Medora seeking a business location.

articles.text: John Sullivan, the world's champion, is beautifying his tonsorial establishment with a coat of paint. John fell from a step-ladder the other day, causing injuries which will necessitate his withdrawing from the pugilistic arena temporarily.
articles.summary: Medora barber John Sullivan painted his shop and was hurt in a fall from a step-ladder.

articles.text: The museum in the Cow Boy office received two valuable additions this week. One was from Vic. Smith, which was a petrified knee joint of a mastodon. The other was donated by J. A. McGregor, and is the finest specimen of petrified wood we have ever seen.
articles.summary: Vic. Smith and J. A. McGregor gave fossils to the Cow Boy office museum.

articles.text: Dr. Fletcher, who has been here on a hunt for some time, left for his home in Indianapolis Monday, and from the amount of baggage and boxes he had we infer he has made a large and valuable collection of curiosities during his stay in the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Dr. Fletcher of Indianapolis left after a long hunt with a collection of Bad Lands curiosities.

articles.text: Two cowboys attempted to paint the usual quiet town of Dickinson red last Thursday. They knocked down an old man, drove women off the street at the point of the revolver, shot one horse dead and badly injured another. One of them enjoyed the extreme pleasure of paying $268 for his amusement.
articles.summary: Two cowboys shot up Dickinson; one was fined $268.

articles.text: The Land Agent is the name of a new paper published at Deadwood. Jas. C. Moody is the editor and proprietor. It is circulated gratuitously, as it is issued in connection with the business of the publisher as a real estate dealer, and its aim is to inform capitalists and investors of the resources and advantages of the Hills.
articles.summary: Jas. C. Moody began The Land Agent, a free real-estate paper at Deadwood.

articles.text: The corner-stone of the new church was laid last Saturday afternoon, and was witnessed by quite a number of people, including the Marquise, who is building the church. On one side of the stone is inscribed "Athenais," and on the other, "Medora, Marquise de Mores, Sept. 15, 1884." The church is being completed as rapidly as possible and in a short time will be ready for services.
articles.summary: The corner-stone of the Medora church being built by the Marquise de Mores was laid.

articles.text: A new mode of communication is being introduced by William Vandriesche, who has sixteen carrier pigeons which he is training to carry messages between this point and the Black Hills. William has made several experiments with them, taking them out to the stage stations, and they have invariably returned in a remarkable short time. It is estimated that they can fly to the Hills in about two or three hours, which is very good time indeed.
articles.summary: William Vandriesche was training carrier pigeons to carry messages between Medora and the Black Hills.

articles.text: Clay Leighton and Henry Scott, the two notorious horse-thieves who were incarcerated in the Dickinson jail upon the charge of stealing horses from Archibald Morton, of South Heart, made their escape Thursday evening. Their absence was not discovered until an hour afterwards, when a posse started in pursuit of the criminals, but up to this writing they have succeeded in evading their pursuers. They made their exit with the assistance of a chisel and a bar of iron eighteen inches long, which was undoubtedly provided them by outside parties.
articles.summary: Accused horse thieves Clay Leighton and Henry Scott escaped the Dickinson jail.

articles.text: Supt. Deffebach returned Tuesday from a trip over the stage route, and informed us that the stages would positively commence running on the morning of October 6. A coach from Deadwood will leave at the same time. The preliminary work has taken up much more time than was anticipated. The proprietors have exercised great care and skillful judgement in equiping the route with the best of everything. The stock is in splendid condition, the stations are nearly all completed and placed in charge of good and responsible parties, and the hungry tourist will not want for a first-class meal when he travels over this route.
articles.summary: Supt. Deffebach announced the Medora–Deadwood stage line would begin running Oct. 6.

articles.summary: Coleman & Brown (Medora Hotel) dissolved; M. M. Coleman continues the business.

articles.text:
Little Tom's Saloon, Little Missouri, Dak. — "There's Rest for the Weary"; "The 'Festive Barkeep' is a mixologist of many years' experience, imported at large expense"; "Every thing from Cow-Boy Bitters to Dude Soda fresh on tap."
J. D. Garver's, Little Missouri, Dak. — Hardware and Tinware; "All kinds of tin and sheet-iron articles made and repaired."
Insurance! Springfield F. & M. Ins. Co., of Springfield, Mass., incorporated 1849 — 36th annual statement, Jan. 1, 1884, gross assets $2,585,633.82; J. N. Dunham, Prest.; S. J. Hall, Sec'y; A. J. Wright, Treas.; Western Department, 148 La Salle St., Chicago, A. J. Harding, General Agent; A. T. Packard, Agent, Bad Lands Cow Boy Office, Medora.
Northern Pacific Railroad — "Going East or Going West"; through line St. Paul to Portland, Ore., Yellowstone National Park.
Brick!! made at the Medora Brick Kiln, "guaranteed better than any brick made in Dakota, or money refunded"; only $8 per thousand; Peter J. Book, Medora, Dak.
Lots! Lots in Medora — price list of town lots by block, for sale at the office of the Bad Lands Cow Boy; A. T. Packard, Medora, Dak.
Beef Cattle — N. P. Ref. Car Co., Medora, Dak., offers its herd of American cattle (about 700 she cattle and 250 steers, plus graded stock) on Beaver creek, Dawson county, Montana.
Mayville Stock Farm, Mayville, Traill Co., Dak. — short-horn bulls; J. L. & E. B. Grandin, Props.; W. W. Warren, General Manager.
Supply Depot for Milwaukee Beer, case, keg or car load — C. B. Williams & Co., Bismarck, Dak.
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, bits, spurs, chaparejos, reatas, quirts, hackamores.
Minneapolis & St. Louis Railway, "Famous Albert Lea Route" (map ad).
Wise & Goodkind, Bismarck, Dak. — wholesale dealers in wines, liquors, cigars, case & bar goods.
